15784-the-chronology-of-ancient-kingdoms:
A work of ancient history by Sir Isaac Newton, printed in London in 1728 after his death. Newton, famous for physics, spent years fitting the reigns of old kings into one timeline. A short chronicle from the first memory of things in Europe to Alexander's conquest of Persia fronts the book. Tonson, Osborn, and Longman published it for learned readers.

Newton tests Greek, Egyptian, and Hebrew records against each other, cutting centuries from received dates. Kings of Egypt, Assyria, and Israel are set in order by reigns, eclipses, and monuments. His method is bold and often wrong by modern lights, yet it shaped debate for a century. The book fascinates as Newton's other life: a natural philosopher trying to fix time itself.
2232-the-duchess-of-malfi:
John Webster's Jacobean tragedy centers on a widowed duchess who secretly marries her steward, defying her powerful brothers. The Duchess of Malfi moves from court intrigue to murder and madness as the brothers' spies close in, and the duchess faces her fate with famous courage. Webster's verse is dark, poetic, and full of skulls, shadows, and whispered plots.

The play is bloody even by its age's standards, yet its heroine's dignity gives it lasting force. Themes of power, gender, and corrupt authority run beneath the horror. For readers of early drama, it stands as one of the great tragedies of the English stage.
24647-the-standard-operaglass-detailed-p:
Charles Annesley compiled this operagoer's guide, in a revised and enlarged edition from the thirty-first to thirty-third thousand, published at London by Sampson Low. It contains the detailed plots of one hundred and fifty-one celebrated operas, with critical and biographical remarks and dates.

Annesley dedicated the book to Therese Malten, the Saxon court singer, whose portrait fronts the volume beside Hans Sachs. Each entry tells the story act by act, so a listener can follow the stage action. Opera lovers will find it a useful companion in the theatre, and a record of the repertory as audiences knew it.
29634-annals-of-music-in-america-a-chron:
Arranged as annals, this chronological record of significant music in America opens with a frank warning: the first hundred years hold very little that would seem important to musicians of today. Yet the record keeps going, year by year, naming works, premieres, and events, from a 1902 piece by C. M. Loeffler to a 1920 work by E. Goossens for string orchestra. Errata on pages 191 and 192 were worked into the text.

The annals form a reference spine for American music history, plain and factual rather than critical. Readers can trace what was heard, when, and where, across two centuries. Students of American music will find a useful, if dry, chronicle that rewards browsing and checking.
31395-railway-adventures-and-anecdotes-e:
Railway Adventures and Anecdotes, extending over more than fifty years and edited by Richard Pike, appeared in a third edition in 1888, published in London and Nottingham. A Liverpool Mercury notice quoted in the book calls it the only genuine railway anecdote book on either side of the Atlantic. Its preface notes how quickly railways changed ideas of speed, recalling a time before them through Niebuhr, the historian in England in 1798.

The anecdotes that follow cover accidents, odd passengers, heroic staff, and the everyday workings of early railways. Pike's collection preserves the folklore of the railway age in the voices of those who lived it. For readers of transport history, it is both entertaining and documentary, a scrapbook of the decades when the train remade travel.
37090-our-knowledge-of-the-external-worl:
Bertrand Russell gave a set of talks first printed in 1914 on how a strict method could renew the study of deep questions. He holds that past work in that field claimed too much and proved too little. Logic, he argues, forms the core of the work, and clear tests should sort what can be known from what can not.

Talks treat our grasp of the world past our senses, and how the world of physics links to the world of sense. Later talks take up endless series, cause, and free will, with old views set out in full. An index ends a book that asks for care and proof at each step.
38513-the-lives-of-the-iii-normans-kings:
The Lives of the III Normans Kings of England, imprinted at London in 1613, gives the reigns of William the First, William the Second and Henrie the First. The book, signed only with its author's initials, is dedicated to Charles, Prince of Wales, and keeps the spelling of its own day.

Its epistle tells how the late Prince Henry, months before his death, called the writer in and complained of English history writing. Able men, Henry said, are busy elsewhere; others fear to write safely of the dead lest the living take offence. Worst of all, base and bungling hands have so soiled the subject that men of quality scorn to touch it.
39158-the-first-seven-divisions-being-a-:
The First Seven Divisions is a detailed account of the fighting from Mons to Ypres in 1914, by Captain Ernest Hamilton, late of the 11th Hussars. A map at the front shows the first seven days of the retreat from Mons. Coloured lines trace the routes each division followed. The days were spent marching, the nights in rest, the map notes.

Chapters cover the battle of Mons, the retreat through Landrecies, and the problem of Le Cateau. The advance to the Aisne and its passage follow. Hamilton writes from inside knowledge of the British Expeditionary Force's first campaign. His book was one of the earliest full accounts of the retreat that saved the army.
44988-alphabetical-catalogue-of-books-in:
The Alphabetical Catalogue of Books in General Literature and Fiction, lists the stock of Chatto and Windus of 111 St Martin's Lane, Charing Cross, London. Entries run by author, with formats and prices. W Davenport Adams's Dictionary of the Drama leads, volume one at 10s 6d net, volume two in preparation.

Grant Allen's novels follow at 3s 6d each in cloth: Babylon, Strange Stories, The Beckoning Hand, Philistia, and The Great Taboo among them. Mrs Alexander's novels, from Valerie's Fate to A Fight with Fate, fill the next entries, and the catalogue runs on through the alphabet.
47290-barney-blake-the-boy-privateer-or-:
Barney Blake, the Boy Privateer, by Herrick Johnstone, is number 1020 of Beadle's Half Dime Library, copyright in February 1897. The weekly cost five cents. Chapter one is called The Ship and Her Crew. Barney Blake tells the tale, a sailor just paid off in Boston.

On a bright May morning in 1813, his old messmate Tony Trybrace calls to him on the wharves. Tony has shipped on a bold privateer, the brigantine Queer Fish. She bears six long guns and a brass swivel gun at her stern. She sails next day for a year at sea. Barney signs on at once, and a boat pulls the pair out to her. A sly old hand sneaks a pull at a bottle as he rows. Boys get a fast dime tale of Yankee sea war.
47501-married-love-a-new-contribution-to:
Married Love, by Marie Carmichael Stopes, stands here in a sixth edition of 1919. Fifield printed it in London. The book first came out on March 26, 1918. Five more editions followed within eleven months, a mark of its fame. Stopes held science doctorates from London and Munich. A preface by Dr Jessie Murray and letters from Professor Starling and a Jesuit father stand at the front. She gives the book to young husbands and all betrothed in love. The subtitle calls it a new contribution to the solving of sex difficulties.

Eleven chapters carry the argument. The Heart's Desire opens, and The Broken Joy follows. Woman's contrariness, the fundamental pulse, and mutual adjustment come next. Sleep, modesty, abstinence, and children take later chapters. Stopes wrote frankly where her age kept silence.
4788-mademoiselle-fifi:
Guy de Maupassant's Mademoiselle Fifi gathers a preface, the title story, and Boule de Suif. Its preface traces Maupassant's life, beginning at the Chateau de Miromesnil near Dieppe, where he was born on August 5, 1850. The Maupassants were an old Lorraine family settled in Normandy in the middle of the eighteenth century, and his father married Laure Le Poittevin in 1846.

With her brother Alfred, Laure had been playmate of Gustave Flaubert, son of a Rouen surgeon, who would direct her son's literary life. A woman of no common literary accomplishments, fond of the classics and especially Shakespeare, she separated from her husband and kept her two sons, Guy and his younger brother Hervé. Until thirteen, Guy lived with his mother at Etretat, between sea and luxuriant country, growing fond of nature and outdoor sports and fishing with fishermen. Readers get two famous Maupassant stories, framed by his boyhood.
49129-father-henson-s-story-of-his-own-l:
Josiah Henson told Father Henson Story of His Own Life, with an introduction by Mrs H B Stowe, issued in Boston by John P Jewett and Company in eighteen fifty eight. The book is headed Truth Stranger than Fiction. Henson was born a slave. Stowe preface calls his record one of the most striking to rise from American slavery.

Born a slave in effect in a heathen land under a heathen master, Henson grew up without Christian light or knowledge. One sermon and one offer of salvation by Christ made him at once a believer and a preacher of Jesus. To forgiveness of enemies and returning good for evil he bore faithful witness, Stowe says. His trials tried men souls, she notes. Henson escaped to Canada, founded a settlement, and preached widely. Readers get a firsthand slave narrative by a model for a famed novel figure.
49927-pearl-fishing-choice-stories-from-:
Pearl-Fishing is an anthology of stories from Dickens's Household Words. The first series was issued at Auburn, New York, in 1854. The publishers explain their aim in a short notice. Household Words had a small reach in America, they say. Its numbers were hard to keep and bind. Many pieces were local or short-lived in interest.

The editors chose the best tales for American homes. The hand of the master shows in them, they claim. The first story, Loaded Dice, opens the set. It tells of a tour through the southern counties of England. The travellers ride in an open carriage. They stop at road-side inns for eggs and milk. Such reprint sets spread Dickens's magazine writing widely. Copyright then gave American houses a free hand. The title promises pearls fished from a deep sea.
50986-glaciers-of-the-rockies-and-selkir:
Coleman, president of the Alpine Club of Canada, wrote this guide to the glaciers of the Rockies and Selkirks for the Dominion Parks Branch. The 1921 edition was republished under the Minister of the Interior, Sir James Lougheed, with notes on five glaciers of the national parks by Wheeler. A photograph of the front of Tumbling Glacier on Berg Lake opens the book.

The traveller, Coleman says, sees glimpses: the train takes the lowest pass, and the ice world lies miles away and thousands of feet above the valley. One must stop at Lake Louise, or Tete Jaune, or Glacier in the Selkirks to touch it. He walks the reader up through thinning forest to timberline at 7,500 feet, where the mountain heathers spread their carpets. The glacial machinery that shaped the surface of Canada is his subject, explained for the tourist with hob-nailed shoes.
51815-henry-smeaton-a-jacobite-story-of-:
George James wrote Henry Smeaton, a Jacobite story of the reign of George the First, published at Paris in 1851 by Galignani for English readers abroad. The novel opens in 1715, the year of the Jacobite rising. James begins beside the water in St James's Square in London, then corrects himself in a playful aside: the pond was there then, whatever later ages did with the square.

A man of twenty-six or twenty-seven watches a boy and girl rowing in a pleasure boat. His dress is sober, plain, and very good, chosen to attract no attention. It is easier to say what he is not than what he is. From that quiet opening the story moves into the plotting of the Fifteen, when supporters of the exiled Stuarts risked everything against the new Hanoverian king. James was a prolific writer of historical romance.
62774-the-renaissance-of-girls-education:
Alice Zimmern of Girton College, Cambridge, wrote this record of fifty years of progress in the schooling of English girls, printed by A D Innes of London in 1898. Zimmern had written Methods of Education in America and Old Tales from Greece. She opens before 1848 and calls the change a renaissance: the revival of an old dream, seen even by Plato.

Chapters trace the first colleges, the high schools, endowments for girls, and the women's colleges. Admission to the universities, boarding schools, technical instruction acts, and state aid follow. Welsh intermediate schools get a chapter of their own. The close, dated 1898, looks at a demand no party dares refuse: schooling for all daughters, rich and poor alike.
67458-the-reign-of-william-rufus-and-the:
The Reign of William Rufus is a history of William the Second of England and the accession of Henry the First, by Edward Freeman. This text is volume one of two, printed at Oxford in 1882. The work carries out the design Freeman set in his History of the Norman Conquest. Its preface promises two sides of those years worked in detail.

One side is their weight for general and constitutional history. The other is their rich store of personal and local narrative. Freeman claims to be the first to deal at length with Bishop William of Saint-Calais. That bishop's career, he argues, matters for the constitution and for understanding Anselm after him. The book is Victorian history at full stretch.
67459-the-reign-of-william-rufus-and-the:
Edward Freeman wrote the reign of William Rufus in two volumes, printed at Oxford in 1882, of which the hosted book is the second. Contents open with chapter five. The wars of Scotland, Northumberland and Wales fill it, from 1093 to 1098. Year by year heads mark the road.

Malcolm of Scotland presses claims at Gloucester in 1093. He sets a stone at Durham abbey, then rides south and is refused a sight of the king. His last raid ends at Alnwick, where Morel slays him that November. Queen Margaret's reforms and the growth of English sway fill the next heads. Mowbray's revolt of 1095 and the placing of Eadgar close the chapter's list.
68758-the-fortunes-of-fifi:
Fortunes of Fifi is a novel by Molly Elliot Seawell, copyright nineteen oh three. Seawell is billed as author of Francezka and Children of Destiny. Pictures by T de Thulstrup go with the text. Its contents run to eleven chapters, from The Imperial Theater to By the Emperor's Order. A picture shows Fifi cuddling her dog Toto.

Chapter one sets Paris in eighteen oh four, on a November night. On the left bank of the Seine the lights were still scarce, the tale says. Three yellow lamps hang on a rope across the narrow Rue du Chat Noir. Tall old rickety houses loom in the brown mist. Across from the theatre stands Cartouche, a general utility man. With him is Mademoiselle Fifi, just promoted to leading lady.
britannica-1911-melfi:
Melfi is a city in Basilicata, Italy, and this 1911 Britannica entry mixes a portrait of the place with its long past. It stands on the lower slopes of Monte Vulture, in the province of Potenza, and held 14,547 people in 1901. Its castle was first raised by Robert Guiscard, though what stands now is mostly the work of the Doria family. The cathedral was founded in 1153 by Robert's son Roger, then rebuilt after an earthquake in 1851 wrecked the town and killed over a thousand people.

The town serves a farming district that yields oil and wine. Its history, as the entry tells it, runs through councils, revolts, and sackings. The Normans made it the capital of Apulia in 1041 and walled it. Later points include a parliament of 1223 under Frederick the Second.
britannica-1911-saffi: Saffi is the subject of a short 1911 Britannica entry on a seaport of Morocco. It is also called Asfi in the text of the entry. The port lies on the west coast, west of Marrakesh. Its folk count is given as about fifteen thousand. It is the chief wool and grain port of central Morocco. Yet its roadstead is open, with no shelter for ships. Talk with the shore can at times be hard. An old palace with fine courts stands above the town.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-amalfi:
Amalfi's archdiocese, directly dependent on the Holy See, sits at Amalfi near Naples, populous between the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries. A free republic from the seventh century to 1075, it matched Pisa and Genoa in prosperity and sea power. It then fell prey to the Normans as one of their chief posts. Emperor Lothair fought there for Innocent II against Sicily's King Roger, who backed Antipope Anacletus.

In medieval culture Amalfi held a worthy place through flourishing schools of law and mathematics. Its republican prosperity, Norman capture, and imperial wars trace a small city's large place in southern Italy's story.
doe-osti-17136589-performance-demonstrat:
Anthony Birri, Holden Hyer, Josh Kendall, and Christian Petrie of Oak Ridge test ways to embed optical fibers inside metal parts, in report ORNL/TM-2026/4815 dated September 2026. A fiber buried in a part can sense strain and heat from within, which suits reactor components. The fiber must survive the making of the part and stay bonded well enough to read truly.

Two routes were tried. Brazing fixed fibers into channels and tubes cut in advance. Directed energy deposition, a metal printing process, built material around the fiber instead. Chapters list materials and gear for each route, then give bonding experiment details and local effects near the fiber. Optical interrogation gear read the fibers during tests, and performance results compare how each route held up.
doe-osti-17197396-performance-demonstrat: Embedded fibers got their performance demo again, and this DOE report covers the manufacturing trials. The pages detail the test results. The composites team gets its proof. The fibers were embedded. The proof was composite. The trials were manufacturing. The proof was composites.
doe-osti-3001264-parametric-analysis-of-:
Max Levien, Giovanni Lozano and Juan Dominguez of Los Alamos test a quiet criticality worry in LA-UR-25-30669, issued 28 October 2025: plutonium dust trapped in air filters. Glovebox work sheds dry plutonium oxide, and local HEPA filters catch it, layer by layer. Enough fissile material in a filter could, in principle, add reactivity. The analysis asks whether credible amounts actually matter, for filters in service, removed in maintenance, or stored inside a glovebox.

History sets the scale: the worst documented filter held 368.8 grams, most under 120, yet the team conservatively modelled 500 grams of plutonium oxide. MCNP6 neutron transport calculations with ENDF/B-VII cross sections examined the credible geometries and conditions under nuclear criticality safety procedure NCS-AP-005. The verdict the document works to validate is that the added reactivity stays insignificant across those cases. The report is the formal calculation record behind that safety claim.
doe-osti-3006118-an-open-benchmark-of-on:
Livermore report LLNL-TR-2013934, dated December 2025, releases an open benchmark of one million cislunar trajectories computed with the SSAPy package. Seven authors are listed: D. Higgins, M. Schneider, K. Pruett, A. Perloff, P. McGill, T. Yeager, and T. Grice. Cislunar space runs from geosynchronous altitude to beyond the Moon. The model includes high-degree Earth and Moon gravity, solar gravity, and radiation pressure from Earth and Sun, leaving out other planets to keep the computing cost down.

Starting conditions sample the orbital element ranges evenly, and each path is propagated for up to six years from one fixed start epoch. The set is offered as a benchmark for development in space domain awareness, navigation, and machine learning, and as a reference library for orbit statistics. The authors report stability trends in the data, including a band near five times geosynchronous radius and some long-lived co-orbital classes.
doe-osti-3009181-wetlands-delineation-re:
Pacific Northwest National Laboratory report PNNL-38536, dated September 2025, delineates wetlands along a planned water and sewer line. Its authors are Dana Vesty and Ioana Bociu. The site is the laboratory's Sequim campus, formerly the Marine Sciences Laboratory. Delineation fixes the legal boundary of a wetland before construction.

Field crews dug soil pits and recorded plant cover in nested plots, 30 feet for trees down to 5 feet for herbs. Worksheets apply the standard dominance test and prevalence index, weighing wetland-loving plants such as western redcedar against upland species. The classifications in the report feed permit decisions for the utility project under county critical areas rules and the Clean Water Act.
doe-osti-3010352-hybrid-learning-techniq:
Machine learning methods that shrink scientific data with error guarantees are covered by Florida's Sanjay Ranka in a closeout report for DOE grant DE-SC0022265. Simulations in fusion, climate, and fluid dynamics turn out tens of petabytes daily, far more than can be kept.

The Guaranteed Autoencoder and the Guaranteed Conditional Diffusion with Tensor Correction frameworks attach explicit error bounds to each rebuilt data set, which plain neural compression cannot promise. A third effort, CAESAR, unifies foundation and generative models for space-time data. Tests on the E3SM climate and S3D combustion data sets beat standard convolutional autoencoders and matched the SZ3 compressor. Keeping derived values true to the source, not just raw fields, is a stated design rule.
doe-osti-3010887-carbstor-development-an:
Pacific Northwest National Laboratory report CarbStor, by Ryan McClure, Marci Garcia, Natalie Sadler, and six co-authors, dated September 2025, builds model soil microbial communities that store carbon. Defined communities, grown in the lab, let researchers assign carbon flows to named microbes instead of guessing at soil's black box.

One community, CSC-A, was profiled as it grew on urea across three time points: inoculation, 24 hours, and 48 hours. Cluster analysis grouped genes that rose and fell together, and pathway enrichment showed which metabolic modules each group carries. Metabolite profiles split sharply between media conditions in the principal component analysis. The work lays groundwork for steering soil communities toward durable carbon storage.
doe-osti-3017113-correct-interpretations:
Dermott E Cullen wrote this Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory report, LLNL-TR-2008244, in July 2025. It corrects how definitions in ENDF-102, the manual for evaluated nuclear data files, should be read for resonance effects. Resonances are energy bands where neutrons interact far more strongly with a nucleus. Getting their treatment wrong distorts reactor and shielding calculations.

Cullen shows how large the differences run. Cross sections computed the corrected way can be up to 100 times higher in the valleys between resonances, and up to 20 times lower near resonance peaks. He supports the point with the tabulated energy grids themselves: uranium-235 carries 743,503 points at zero kelvin, and uranium-238 carries 1,787,916. Data evaluators and code writers get a warning backed by counts: a definition read casually can shift answers by orders of magnitude.
doe-osti-3018737-sierra-multimechanics-m:
Sandia's SIERRA Thermal/Fluid Development Team issued this verification manual, SAND2026-16585, printed January 27, 2026. Aria is Sierra's multimechanics module, handling coupled thermal, fluid, and chemical problems. The manual documents the version 5.28 verification suite. Its structure is deliberately repetitive. Each test names the features exercised, the boundary conditions, and the material parameters. A verification-of-solution section then compares the computed result with the known answer. Basic thermal tests open the book: steady heat conduction on Hex8, Hex20, and Hex27 meshes.

Running the same physics on three element types isolates discretization error from modeling error. Input decks appear in the text, down to solver settings and surface definitions. That candor lets an outside analyst rerun any test exactly. Hundreds of pages of such tests are unglamorous. They are also the reason a regulator can accept an Aria result. The manual is the audit trail for one release of the code.
doe-osti-3020533-testing-of-prototype-pv:
National Laboratory of the Rockies CRADA final report NLR/TP-5K00-99002, CRD-20-16876, with Peter Hacke as technical contact, reports durability testing of prototype solar modules from SunFlex, a finalist in DOE's American-Made Solar Prize. Before a new module design can sell, it must survive standardized stress tests. The laboratory ran the temperature cycling and damp heat sequences of IEC 61215 and the potential-induced degradation sequence of IEC 62804-1.

Testing used six four-cell modules for the first task set. One set of modules lost about 2 percent relative fill factor through temperature cycling, a change tied to rising series resistance. Another set showed negligible degradation. Plans for sixty-cell module testing were set aside in favor of additional combined accelerated stress testing. The results give the manufacturer evidence on how its prototypes age under heat, moisture, and electrical stress.
doe-osti-3021518-comstock-measure-docume:
NLR report NLR/TP-5500-98224, by Janghyun Kim and Chris CaraDonna, documents a ComStock modeling measure. The measure swaps standard rooftop air-conditioning units for high-efficiency models across the United States commercial building stock. ComStock is DOE's model of the national building fleet, and this document records how the upgrade was defined, which buildings qualify, and how cooling and heating performance curves were built.

Modeled across the whole stock, the upgrade cuts electricity use by 9.2 percent and total site energy by 7.8 percent, while gas and oil use tick slightly upward from changed heating patterns. In buildings that actually qualify for the upgrade, total savings reach 16 percent. Savings concentrate in hot climates: in climate zone 1A, typical buildings saved between roughly 10 and 30 percent on utility bills.
doe-osti-3022396-development-of-lighting:
A Pennsylvania State University final report by Dorukalp Durmus, under DOE award DE-EE0009690, develops a fairer way to judge lighting efficiency. The standard metric, luminous efficacy, rates the lamp alone; it says nothing about how much of that light actually reaches the surfaces and eyes that need it in a real room. The project defines lighting application efficacy to close that gap, relating electrical power consumed to light that contributes to occupants' visual perception.

The framework follows light along its path: emitted by the luminaire, traveling through the space, and entering the visual system. Ray-tracing software estimates what fraction lands on task areas and visual fields. A spreadsheet tool lets practitioners compute the metric. Human perception experiments, including two-alternative forced-choice brightness tests, ground the visual side of the framework.
doe-osti-3022817-evaluation-of-three-typ:
LLNL report LLNL-TR-2010642, by Xianjin Yang with William Junor of Los Alamos, compares three kinds of electric-field sensors side by side. The sensors, capacitive electrodes, porous pots, and stainless-steel stakes, are the workhorses of electromagnetic monitoring stations. The evaluation on June 3 and 4, 2025 asked which produces the cleanest record of the same field.

At two stations the three types tracked each other closely on the east component, with porous pot and stainless stake showing similar, correlated signatures. Noise separated them. The capacitive electrode sensors at one station produced strong noise pulses every five seconds in both horizontal components, severe enough that the units went back to the vendor for troubleshooting and repair. Porous pot and stake records were the least noisy overall, giving station operators a clear procurement steer.
doe-osti-3030659-hydromine-simple-modula:
Carsten H. Westergaard of Westergaard Solutions leads the HydroMINE final report under ARPA-E award DE-AR0001440, dated October 2025, with Ike Udoh and Sandia co-investigator Brent Houchens on the team. HydroMINE pulls power from moving water. Its outer face meets the flow with a fully passive sweeping surface, so the unit has no exposed spinning rotor for debris or ice to wreck. Units can float or sit fixed, alone or in groups.

The reporting period ran from December 2021 to February 2024. The team shaped four use cases, from sheltered water to harsh open sites, and wrote a design basis covering debris, ice, and water level swings. For each case they produced scalable concept designs and picked the best to refine. Simple stress checks proved plentiful for the milder cases, the report notes.
doe-osti-3367083-sierra-multimechanics-m:
Sandia National Laboratories report SAND2026-21788 is the verification manual for Sierra/Aria version 5.30, printed May 21, 2026 by the Sierra Thermal/Fluid Development Team. Aria simulates heat flow and fluid physics inside Sandia's Sierra multimechanics framework. Verification problems compare the code against solutions known by construction, catching errors before the code is trusted on real hardware.

The opening suites run steady heat conduction on eight-node and twenty-node hexahedral meshes, checking boundary conditions and material parameters case by case. Manufactured-solution tests compute error norms for temperature and its gradient, with precision settings recorded in the input decks. Hundreds of documented cases form the regression net for the thermal-fluid code. Analysts consult the manual to see exactly which physics each release has proven.
doe-osti-3376154-memorial-pools-energy-e:
The final technical report for Department of Energy award DE-EE0010708 covers energy retrofits at the National September 11 Memorial and Museum in New York. Marc Mancini, the museum's engineering vice president, led the project. The award period ran from September to December 2025, though the field work wrapped up in August. The target was the Memorial Pools, the twin reflecting pools that mark the towers' footprints. Their wall lights were due for an efficiency upgrade.

Crews pulled the pool wall fixtures in two rounds. Each batch was shipped to Minnesota, retrofitted there, and sent back for reinstallation. The second round closed on August 27, 2025. That date marked one hundred percent completion of the last milestone, numbered 4.2. No no-go milestones were hit on the way. With the build done by the second quarter, the report notes no work remains for later quarters.
doe-osti-3409361-computational-analysis-:
Argonne report ANL-26/36, by M. Sitek, models how well Michigan DOT drainage covers J and K catch road runoff. These covers combine a grate with a curb opening window. Road crews need inlets that drain lanes without flooding.

Simulations varied gutter flow rates and road slopes. For both covers, grate capture rose steadily as gutter flow grew. The curb window added capture on top of the grate share. Slope cases ran from 0.003 to 0.05 feet per foot in the chart discussed. Highway engineers can size and place inlets with modeled proof instead of rules of thumb alone.
doe-osti-3943090-facilitating-the-use-of:
Rudeger H. T. Wilke and Jonathan Smith of Sandia National Laboratories test whether language models can move test code between formats without losing meaning. Their report, SAND2026-26615, was printed in October 2026. Test shops store test steps in a shared format called ATML, while many labs write tests in plain Python code.

Early chapters explain the ATML format and how it marks parts that any test language can share. The team then fed Python test scripts to a language model and asked for standard-form output. One snag stood out: the model flagged valid calls as errors when it lacked the class text behind them, so the fix was to give the model that text as context. Vote tricks could not cure the fault, since the same wrong idea repeats. The work points to a faster path for shared test libraries.
mademoiselle-fifi:
Mademoiselle Fifi is a book of stories by Guy de Maupassant. A preface here tells his life, from his birth in 1850 near Dieppe. His mother, Laure, had played with Gustave Flaubert as a girl. Flaubert later guided her son's first steps in writing.

Young Guy grew up at Etretat, between sea and green country. The title tale is set in the Franco-Prussian War. A slight, fair Prussian officer is nicknamed Mademoiselle Fifi by his comrades. 'Boule de Suif,' his most famous story, stands beside it. Maupassant's tales are clear, cold, and perfectly made. Few writers have matched his art of the short story.
nasa-tm-19650012596-an-evaluation-of-the:
W E Daniels, Shirley J Hendricks, and Duane C Jensen at Goddard produced this December 1964 evaluation of Earth's main magnetic field. It covers the years 1940 to 1962. Their work rests on magnetic survey data and on yearly mean values from observatories around the world.

A good field model matters for navigation, for spacecraft work, and for science. Earth's field changes slowly over time, so old data must be combined with care. The authors build a new determination of the field from that long record. Readers get both the result and the data base behind it, spanning more than two decades.
nasa-tm-19680016262-determination-of-the:
Reuven Ramaty of Goddard Space Flight Center and Richard E. Lingenfelter of the University of California at Los Angeles wrote this May 1968 preprint, X-611-68-208. Their topic is a Type IV solar radio burst, a strong radio outburst from high in the Sun's outer air, called the corona. From that one signal they seek the corona's magnetic field and the energy of its radio-emitting electrons.

The pair calculate how fast electrons spiraling in a magnetic field give off radio waves, called gyro-synchrotron emission. They show the burst's sharp low and high frequency cutoffs fit that process in ionized gas. Given the gas density near the burst, the observed spectrum then yields both the field strength and the electron energy range.
nasa-tm-19680017934-an-experimental-stud:
Roy L. Marshall, Gerald L. Pellett, and Andrew R. Saunders of Langley Research Center measured the drag of burning aluminum droplets in this study, presented in October 1966. Burning particles move through many combustion systems, so their motion matters. The team watched droplets between about 200 and 500 microns wide as they burned.

The droplets fell through still ambient air while burning. The team tracked their motion to find the effective drag force on each one. Their starting idea was that a burning droplet feels quite different drag than a cold one. The results feed models of multi-phase combustion flows. Such models guide the design of burners and rocket systems using metal fuels.
nasa-tm-19700008713-current-density-mapp:
Robert M. Masters and Francis J. Stenger of the Lewis Research Center studied cadmium sulfide thin-film solar cells. Such cells can lose power where the current flows unevenly. Their report presents a fast way to find those weak spots.

The method measures the magnetic field just above the face of the cell. From those readings it draws a map of where the current runs strong or weak. The map is shown in graphic form, so uneven regions can be seen at a glance. A quick check of this kind helps makers spot flawed cells early.
nasa-tm-19710007024-evaluation-of-linear:
Richard J. Mittendorf of the Lewis Research Center wrote this report in February 1971. It evaluates two plastics for use as irradiation capsules. Sealed capsules hold experiments while they are exposed to radiation in a reactor.

Both capsule types were irradiated inside metal containers at the Plum Brook Reactor. The goal was to fix the safe working limits for each plastic. Limits for the polyethylene capsules were defined by the tests, Mittendorf reports. The epoxy capsules turned highly radioactive under exposure. They also failed at lower exposure levels than the polyethylene ones.
nasa-tm-19710008960-space-shuttle-auxili: Space Shuttle Auxiliary Propulsion Configurations and Technology is the title of a NASA technical memorandum. It covers the small hydrogen and oxygen propulsion systems planned for the space shuttle orbiter and booster. The catalog record ties the report to auxiliary propulsion design choices and the technology behind them. The hosted sample, however, preserves only a reproduction notice and garbled scan pages. No author, center, date, or readable abstract survives in the sample, so the report's detailed contents cannot be described from the evidence provided.
podcast-tuckercarlson-5x9vR5sKHFI:
Tucker Carlson devotes this episode to what he calls the secret history of the Bible's strangest figures. They are the giants and demons of scripture. He also covers the advanced civilizations he says flourished before the Great Flood destroyed them. The discussion treats the early chapters of Genesis as a suppressed record rather than myth.

Carlson and his material move between the biblical text, ancient sources, and modern alternative archaeology. The flood story appears in many cultures, and the episode leans on that spread as evidence of a real, shared memory. Mainstream scholars read these texts differently, and listeners should know the claims are contested. Preserved here is a popular broadcaster's full argument that the ancient world was stranger, and better informed, than the modern one admits.
the-chronology-of-ancient-kingdoms-amend:
Sir Isaac Newton wrote this work on ancient dates, printed in London in 1728 for J. Tonson, J. Osborn, and T. Longman. Its title promises an amended chronology of ancient kingdoms, with a short chronicle prefixed. That chronicle runs from the first memory of things in Europe to Alexander the Great's conquest of Persia.

A dedication to the Queen presents the book as Newton's last work. The writer of that address calls it an offering from as great a genius as any age has produced. He notes the Queen's steady support for arts and sciences, and the many honors she had shown the author. On those grounds, he argues, this work above the rest claims her protection. Readers get Newton's late attempt to rebuild the timeline of the ancient world on stricter evidence, compressing reigns that older histories had stretched far too long.
the-duchess-of-malfi:
John Webster's tragedy The Duchess of Malfi comes with a front note on the playwright's dim life. His birth and death dates are mere guesses, the note says; he first shows up in 1602 writing plays with others for Henslowe. Four plays are his alone, and this one was printed in 1623, though it may have been writ as early as 1611.

Drawn from Bandello through Painter, the plot shows a widowed duchess who weds her steward in secret. Her brothers' rage brings spies, madness, and death. Webster's dark verse still chills the stage.
